summary: Revises RFC 2086, which lets IMAP mailbox access control lists be read and changed over the protocol. It defines several new access control rights and clarifies which rights are needed for different IMAP commands. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A way to say who may look at, change, or delete things in a shared mailbox, like keys given to different people.

subtitle: How an IMAP server describes who may do what to each mailbox, and how clients read and change those permissions.

tldr.problem: Shared mailboxes need permissions, but RFC 2086 left ambiguities: which rights each IMAP command needs, how non-ASCII identifiers work, and how rights relate to READ-WRITE and READ-ONLY.
tldr.mechanism: Each mailbox gets an access control list of identifier and rights pairs, managed with SETACL, DELETEACL, GETACL, LISTRIGHTS and MYRIGHTS. Single-letter rights such as l, r, w, i and a are tied to specific IMAP commands.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 2086 with finer rights (t, e, k, x) and keeps the old d and c rights as virtual rights so older clients still work.

facts.label: Capability
facts.value: ACL, plus RIGHTS= for extra rights

today: RFC 4314 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2005. It obsoletes RFC 2086, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the ACL Extension Does
sections.content:
The ACL extension lets an IMAP client retrieve and manipulate mailbox access control lists through the IMAP protocol itself. A server advertises it by returning ACL among its capabilities.

RFC 4314 is a revision of RFC 2086. It tries to clear up ambiguities in the old text, in particular the use of UTF-8 in access identifiers, which rights are required for different IMAP commands, and how the READ-WRITE and READ-ONLY response codes relate to the ACL.
sections.eli5: It is the rulebook for sharing an email folder: who is allowed to do what with it. The old rulebook was fuzzy in places, so this one cleans it up.

sections.title: Identifiers, Rights and the Standard Rights
sections.content:
An access control list is a set of identifier, rights pairs that applies to one mailbox name. An identifier is a UTF-8 string. The identifier anyone means everybody, including anonymous users. Any user name accepted by LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE is reserved for that user. Identifiers starting with a dash are reserved for negative rights, and other strings are interpreted in an implementation-defined way.

Rights are a string of alphanumeric characters, each standing for a set of controlled operations. Lowercase letters are reserved for standard rights and can only be extended by a standards-track document. Digits are for implementation- or site-defined rights. Uppercase rights are not allowed.

An identifier such as -fred is a negative right. Granting -fred the w right removes w from user fred, even if another entry would give it. This differs from DELETEACL, which just removes an entry. Servers are not required to support negative rights.

When several identifiers apply to one user (the user, a group, anyone), how their rights are combined is implementation defined. A server may take the union, or use only the most specific entry. A server may also tie rights together, so that they are granted all or none. Clients find out what is possible with LISTRIGHTS and what they have with MYRIGHTS.

A server that conforms to this document MUST also list rights beyond the ones from RFC 2086 in a RIGHTS= capability.

The standard rights

The standard rights each map to a group of IMAP operations. The most commonly checked are l (lookup, so the mailbox shows up in LIST and LSUB), r (read, so you can SELECT and run STATUS) and i (insert, so you can APPEND or COPY into it).

Three flag rights split the message flags: s keeps the seen or unseen state across sessions, t controls the \Deleted flag, and w controls every other flag. Mailbox-level rights are k (create sub-mailboxes), x (delete the mailbox), e (EXPUNGE) and a (administer the ACL). The p right is for posting mail to the submission address of the mailbox and is not enforced by IMAP itself.
sections.eli5:
The list has names and the keys each name holds. A name with a dash in front means "take these keys away from this person", even if someone else's entry would give them.

Each letter is one key: one lets you see the folder, one lets you read, one lets you add things, one lets you throw things away, and one lets you change the key list.

sections.title: Virtual Rights d and c for Old Clients
sections.content:
RFC 2086 was ambiguous, so some servers used c to control DELETE and others used d. RFC 4314 splits those: k controls CREATE and x controls DELETE, while e and t control expunging and marking messages deleted. The old d and c survive as virtual rights that are macros for the new ones.

If a client sends d, the server MUST treat it as every member of the "delete" right. If any member is set, the server MUST also include d when returning rights in MYRIGHTS or ACL responses, and likewise for c. This keeps RFC 2086 clients working with newer servers. Clients that conform to RFC 4314 MUST ignore the virtual d and c in responses. The RIGHTS= capability MUST NOT list the rights defined in RFC 2086.

Appendix B suggests two routes for old servers: tie t, e and possibly x together with almost no changes, or implement them separately and return d when any is granted.
sections.eli5: The old keys d and c were big keys that opened several locks. The new rules cut them into smaller keys, but the server still hands out the big ones so old email programs do not get confused.

sections.title: The ACL Commands and Responses
sections.content:
Five commands manage ACLs. SETACL takes a mailbox, an identifier and a rights string. A plus prefix adds rights, a minus prefix removes them, and no prefix replaces them. An unrecognized right MUST cause a BAD response, never silent ignoring. DELETEACL removes the entry for an identifier. GETACL returns the whole list in an untagged ACL response. LISTRIGHTS returns the rights always granted and the groups of tied optional rights that could be granted to an identifier. MYRIGHTS returns the rights the current user has.

For commands that take an identifier (SETACL, DELETEACL, LISTRIGHTS) servers SHOULD first prepare it with the SASLprep profile of stringprep. If that fails or gives an empty string, the server MUST refuse with BAD. A GETACL response MAY show a canonical form of an identifier, but a LISTRIGHTS response MUST return the identifier exactly as the client sent it, so the client can match it to the command.
sections.eli5: There are five requests: change the list, remove a name, show the whole list, ask what could be given to someone, and ask what I am allowed to do myself.

sections.title: Rights Required by Each IMAP Command
sections.content:
Before running a command, an ACL server MUST check the rights it needs. Section 4 gives a table and then the detailed rules. For example, LIST needs l but must never answer NO for a mailbox it cannot list. SELECT, EXAMINE and STATUS need r. EXPUNGE needs e, and CLOSE without e simply skips the expunge and returns OK. SETACL, DELETEACL, GETACL and LISTRIGHTS need a. MYRIGHTS needs at least one of l, r, i, k, x or a.

CREATE needs k on the nearest existing parent, and the new mailbox SHOULD inherit the parent's ACL. DELETE needs x, and DELETE MUST delete the mailbox's ACL. RENAME needs x on the mailbox and k on the new parent, and SHOULD NOT change the ACLs.

For COPY and APPEND the target needs i. Then each message flag is kept only if the user holds the matching right: t for \Deleted, s for \Seen, w for the rest. The server MUST NOT fail the whole operation because a flag was dropped. STORE uses the same flag-to-right mapping and SHOULD NOT fail if at least one flag can be changed.
sections.eli5: Each action has its own key. Copying a message into a folder needs the "add" key, but if you lack the "trash" key, the copy just arrives without its trash mark.

sections.title: Server and Client Rules
sections.content:
Servers MUST list the extra rights in the RIGHTS= capability, and that set MUST include t, e, x and k, for example RIGHTS=texk. Servers MUST accurately reflect the current user's rights in FLAGS and PERMANENTFLAGS responses. A client MAY pipeline SELECT and MYRIGHTS for speed.

A server MAY cache rights when a mailbox is selected, so changes made by SETACL or DELETEACL may not apply until the mailbox is re-selected. If a server changes other ACLs as a side effect of SETACL or DELETEACL, it MUST send untagged ACL responses to tell the client. A SETACL followed by MYRIGHTS in a pipeline is an ambiguity, so the server must finish SETACL first.

A client that can read and update ACLs but does not let the user edit rights it does not recognize MUST preserve those rights, so it does not remove permissions it does not understand.

For SELECT, the server MUST send READ-ONLY if the user has none of i, e or the "shared flag rights" (the flag rights of flags shared between users on that mailbox). It SHOULD send READ-WRITE if the user has at least one of them.
sections.eli5: Servers must say which extra keys exist and be honest about which ones you hold. Email programs must not throw away keys they do not recognize when they save the list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ACL commands MUST NOT leak information about mailboxes with restricted ACLs. If a user runs GETACL on a mailbox they cannot LIST, the server answers with the same error as for a mailbox that does not exist.

Clients that can modify ACLs SHOULD warn a user who wants to give full access, or even just the a right, to the identifier anyone. Servers MAY reject identifiers containing character sequences affected by a known Unicode normalization anomaly, with a tagged BAD. ACL information is sent in the clear unless confidentiality protection such as STARTTLS or negotiated privacy in AUTHENTICATE is used.
sections.eli5: Do not let people learn that a private folder exists just by asking about it, and warn anyone who is about to give the keys to everybody.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2086 and Known Gaps
sections.content:
Appendix A lists 24 changes. Among them: identifiers moved from US-ASCII to UTF-8, DELETE is controlled by x and EXPUNGE by e, new rights t and k were added, a now also covers DELETEACL, r now also covers STATUS, and GETACL is explicitly not allowed with only r, because it could reveal which identifiers exist on the mail system.

Appendix C admits known deficiencies. There is no equivalent of chown and chgrp for Unix-style rights bits. Because rights combination is implementation defined, building a friendly interface is hard. Users, groups and special identifiers share one namespace. The text mentions a work-in-progress "ACL2" extension that might eventually supersede this one, but says RFC 2086 was deployed in multiple implementations, so this backward-compatible step was considered worthwhile.
sections.eli5: The new rulebook fixes lots of small problems from the old one and honestly lists a few that are still not solved.

items.label: lookup
items.desc: Mailbox is visible to LIST and LSUB, and can be subscribed.

items.label: read
items.desc: SELECT the mailbox and perform STATUS.

items.label: write
items.desc: Set or clear flags other than \Seen and \Deleted.

items.label: insert
items.desc: Perform APPEND and COPY into the mailbox.

items.label: post
items.desc: Send mail to the submission address; not enforced by IMAP.

items.label: delete mailbox
items.desc: DELETE the mailbox; old name in RENAME.

items.label: expunge
items.desc: EXPUNGE, and expunge as part of CLOSE.
